title: Wise Words
subtitle: WITH MARCO REYES  ·  STORY NIGHT

segments.head: TONIGHT: THE PUMPKIN WAR
segments.author: Wise Words
lines: Good evening, everyone.
I'm Marco Reyes, and this is Wise Words.
Tonight's story is about Marcus Bell, a tow truck driver from Nampa, Idaho.
For eleven years, his neighbor Gene won the county fair blue ribbon for the biggest pumpkin.
And hung it on his porch, right where Marcus could see it.

segments.head: CHAPTER 1: THE RIBBON
segments.quote: As iron is eaten away by rust, so the envious are consumed by their own passion.
segments.author: Antisthenes
lines: Marcus grumbled about that ribbon every morning.
His wife Tanya pointed at the rust on his tow truck, and quoted Antisthenes, a Greek philosopher:
As iron is eaten away by rust, so the envious are consumed by their own passion.
Marcus looked at his own frown in the window. Then he ordered a thirty-dollar pumpkin seed.

segments.head: CHAPTER 2: THE DIRT
segments.quote: A garden is a grand teacher. It teaches patience and careful watchfulness; it teaches industry and thrift; above all, it teaches entire trust.
segments.author: Gertrude Jekyll
lines: Marcus knew engines, not dirt. He thought fertilizer was a soda.
At the library, he found a book by Gertrude Jekyll, a famous English gardener:
A garden is a grand teacher. It teaches patience and careful watchfulness; it teaches industry and thrift; above all, it teaches entire trust.
So he checked every leaf at five a.m. Tanya said he talked to that vine more than to her.

segments.head: CHAPTER 3: YELLOW LEAVES
segments.quote: Pride costs us more than hunger, thirst and cold.
segments.author: Thomas Jefferson
lines: In July, the big leaves turned yellow. Marcus panicked.
The only man who knew why lived next door. Marcus remembered Thomas Jefferson:
Pride costs us more than hunger, thirst and cold.
So he knocked on Gene's door. Gene poured two coffees and said, son, you're drowning it.

segments.head: CHAPTER 4: THE HAIL
segments.quote: Everybody talks about the weather, but nobody does anything about it.
segments.author: Charles Dudley Warner
lines: In August came hail the size of golf balls.
Gene stood on his porch, quoting the writer Charles Dudley Warner:
Everybody talks about the weather, but nobody does anything about it.
Marcus did something. He grabbed the tarps from his tow truck and covered Gene's pumpkin first.
His own got three dents. He called them dimples.

segments.head: CHAPTER 5: THE WEIGH-OFF
segments.quote: When you're good to others, you are best to yourself.
segments.author: Benjamin Franklin
lines: At the fair, Gene's pumpkin weighed six hundred and twelve pounds. Marcus's, six hundred and ten.
Two pounds. About three dimples. It stung.
Then he remembered Benjamin Franklin's old almanac:
When you're good to others, you are best to yourself.
So Marcus cheered for Gene louder than anybody in Idaho.

segments.head: CHAPTER 6: THE GATE
segments.quote: Each friend represents a world in us, a world possibly not born until they arrive.
segments.author: Anaïs Nin
lines: That night, Gene hung the ribbon on Marcus's fridge and said, eleven years, and nobody to talk pumpkins with.
Marcus thought of the writer Anais Nin:
Each friend represents a world in us, a world possibly not born until they arrive.
Next spring, they cut a gate in the fence, and grew one pumpkin together.

segments.head: THAT'S TONIGHT'S STORY
segments.quote: Drop the envy. Learn. Ask. Act. Be good to others. Open the gate.
segments.author: Marco Reyes
lines: That's tonight's story.
Let go of envy. Learn. Ask for help. Do something. Be good to others. Open the gate.
I grew a tomato once. The squirrels threw it a party.
I'm Marco Reyes. Good night.
